property_summary: If this test contract successfully calls lockInGuess with a provided wei value, then the contract's recorded guess slot for this caller becomes nonzero (i.e., block number stored != 0).
If a call to lockInGuess with amount X reverts, then X is not equal to 1 ether (i.e., only sending exactly 1 ether succeeds on the original contract).
On the original contract, calling lockInGuess succeeds exactly when the caller sends 1 ether (i.e., reverted is false iff amount == 1 ether).

On the original contract, any call to lockInGuess that succeeds (does not revert) must be made with exactly 1 ether; the mutant rejects some of those successful calls (e.g. it requires 2 ether) so there exist inputs where reverted == false but amount != 2 ether.
Any call to lockInGuess that succeeds (does not revert) must send exactly 1 ether (so reverted == false implies amount == 1 ether).

For any caller and any 32-byte guess hash, the reference contract accepts lockInGuess when the caller sends exactly 1 ether (call succeeds) and records a nonzero stored block; the mutant instead requires 2 ether so for some fuzzed (caller, amount) combinations the call will revert and no guess is recorded — we assert that sending exactly 1 ether always results in a successful lockInGuess on the reference (but would fail on the mutant for some inputs).

For any caller and any 32-byte guess, calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference C and records a nonzero scheduled block; the mutant that changes the require to 2 ether will cause such calls with 1 ether to revert for some callers/inputs, breaking this property.

For any caller and any guess hash, calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether always succeeds (does not revert) on the reference contract C (so the call returns normally), but the mutant that changes the require to 2 ether will cause such calls with 1 ether to revert for some inputs (i.e., the call may fail); the test fuzzes caller and guess and asserts that the call succeeds on the reference.

For any caller and any 32-byte guess, if the caller sends either 1 ether or 2 ether then exactly one of these two payments will succeed on the reference contract (specifically, sending 1 ether succeeds and records a guess while sending 2 ether reverts because the reference requires 1 ether), whereas the mutant that changes the require to 2 ether will accept 2 ether instead and thus there exist inputs where the success pattern across the two amounts differs; we assert that on the reference, calling lockInGuess with 1 ether succeeds (non-reverting) and calling with 2 ether reverts (so exactly one of the two succeeds) for all callers/guesses — a property the mutant violates for some inputs.

For any caller and any 32-byte guess, calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether on the reference C always succeeds (does not revert) and thus returns normally; the mutant that changes the required msg.value to 2 ether will cause some of these same calls (with 1 ether) to revert, breaking this property.

For any caller that calls lockInGuess with 1 ether when they have no pending guess, the contract sets their stored guesses[msg.sender].block to a non-zero value and does not allow overwriting an existing non-zero block; the mutant that removes the prior-zero check permits overwriting an existing guess (changing stored block) and thus violates the 'cannot overwrite existing active guess' rule for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with 1 ether when they have no prior guess, the recorded guesses(msg.sender).block in the reference contract is strictly greater than the current block.number at the time of the call (i.e., equals block.number+1), whereas the mutant records it as block.number causing guesses(msg.sender).block == block.number, breaking that invariant for some inputs.

After a successful lockInGuess by any caller sending exactly 1 ether with no prior guess, the recorded guesses(msg.sender).block is strictly greater than the block number at which lockInGuess was called (i.e., reference sets block.number+1) — the mutant that sets it to block.number violates this for some inputs.

For any caller who freshly locks a guess by calling lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether, the reference contract records guesses[caller].block strictly greater than the block number at which the call executed (block.number+1); the mutant that writes block.number instead records it equal to the current block and thus violates that invariant for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess(addressed by a fuzzed actor) sending exactly 1 ether with no prior guess, the reference contract records guesses[actor].block > block.number at the time of observation (it stores block.number+1), whereas the mutant that stores block.number can produce guesses[actor].block == block.number for some inputs, violating this invariant.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether and no prior guess, the reference contract records guesses[caller].block strictly greater than the block number at which the observation is made (it stores block.number+1); the mutant that stores block.number can produce recorded block equal to the current block for some fuzzed actor/tx ordering, violating this rule.

After a caller successfully calls lockInGuess(hash) paying 1 ether, the stored guess for that caller equals the exact hash they provided (i.e., guesses[msg.sender].guess == hash); the mutant inverts the stored bytes and thus violates this for many hashes.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess(hash) paying 1 ether, the contract stores exactly the provided bytes32 hash for that caller (the mutant stores the bitwise inverted hash, so for many fuzzed hashes the stored value will differ).

For any actor and any bytes32 guess, after calling lockInGuess with 1 ether the public getter for the stored guess (guesses(actor).guess) equals the provided bytes32; the mutant that XORs with all-ones will cause the stored getter to differ for some inputs.

For every caller and every bytes32 input, after a successful lockInGuess call paying 1 ether the stored getter guesses(caller).guess is either equal to the provided hash or equal to its bitwise inverse; the reference always stores the exact provided hash (so guesses(caller).guess == hash) while the mutant sometimes stores the inverted value, violating that equality for those inputs.

For any caller and any bytes32 input, after calling lockInGuess paying 1 ether the contract's public getter for guesses(caller).guess equals the exact bytes32 provided; the mutant that XORs with all-ones stores the inverted bytes, so for some fuzzed hashes the getter will differ.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess with exactly 1 ether and no prior guess, the stored guesses(msg.sender).guess equals the hash argument after the call (reference preserves final stored guess = provided hash); the mutant that resets guess to zero before writing can be observed via reentrancy during the call and thus can transiently differ causing some observable behavior to break this rule.

For any caller who successfully calls lockInGuess(msgHash) with exactly 1 ether and no prior guess, after the call completes the stored guess for that caller equals msgHash; the mutant that writes zero before writing the hash can be observed by a reentrant attacker during the call and thus causes a difference (the reentrant observation can see a zero transiently), so deploying a reentrant helper and fuzzing the hash and caller will find inputs where the mutant violates this rule.

For any caller X and any guess hash H, after calling lockInGuess(H) with exactly 1 ether when X had no prior guess, the stored guess for X equals H (reference preserves final stored value), whereas the mutant that writes zero then H can be observed by a reentrant callee during lockInGuess leading to a state-visible transient zero that breaks this invariant for some inputs when a reentrant helper is used.

For any caller who calls lockInGuess(hash) with exactly 1 ether and had no prior guess, the contract's public getter for guesses(caller).guess equals the provided hash after the call; the mutant that writes zero before storing the hash can be observed by a reentrant callee during lockInGuess and thus can cause a differing observed value for some inputs.

For any caller who had no prior guess, after calling lockInGuess(hash) with exactly 1 ether the public getter guesses(caller).guess equals the provided hash; the mutant that writes zero then the hash can be observed by a reentrant callee mid-call causing the getter to return a different value during reentrancy, so a reentrant attacker can make the mutant violate this rule for some fuzzed inputs.

After a successful settle call (caller paid 1 ether previously and block progressed so blockhash is available), the reference contract always clears the stored guess.block to zero, whereas the mutant leaves it nonzero by setting it to current block number.

For any caller who previously locked a guess and then calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always resets their stored guesses[msg.sender].block to zero; the mutant sets it to the current block number, leaving it nonzero for some inputs.

For any caller who has previously locked a guess and then successfully calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always clears guesses[msg.sender].block to zero; the mutant may leave it nonzero by setting it to the current block number.

For any caller who previously locked a guess, after calling settle the reference implementation always sets their stored guesses[msg.sender].block to 0 (clears it); the mutant instead sometimes leaves it nonzero by setting it to the current block number, violating this clearing property.

For any address that has locked a guess, after calling settle() the reference implementation always resets that caller's stored guesses[msg.sender].block to 0, whereas the mutant sets it to the current block number (nonzero) for some inputs so the cleared-block property is violated.

For any player who locks a guess and later calls settle, the reference contract clears their stored block (making it zero) after settle returns; the mutant fails to clear it so the stored block remains nonzero for some inputs (allowing repeated payouts or differing state).

After any call to settle by a player who had previously lockInGuess'd and when block.number advances past the locked block, the reference contract always resets guesses[player].block to 0 (so repeated settle calls do not keep the stored block), whereas the mutant that omits that reset can leave guesses[player].block nonzero — allowing the state (the stored block) to differ after settle.

For any caller that has locked a guess and then calls settle after the target block has passed, the reference contract always clears guesses[caller].block to 0 (so address(c).balance cannot be drained repeatedly from repeated successful settles without re-locking), whereas the mutant that omits resetting guesses[caller].block can leave that stored block nonzero and allow differing behavior/state after settle (detectable by repeated settle attempts/payments).

After a successful call to settle, the contract always clears the caller's stored guess.block to 0 (so repeated settle calls cannot attempt to reuse the same locked guess), whereas the mutant increments the stored block instead, leaving a nonzero value and thus breaking this property for some inputs.

For any caller who successfully called lockInGuess and then settle when block.number > storedBlock, the reference contract resets guesses[caller].block to 0 after settle completes; the mutant instead decrements the stored block (nonzero for some inputs), so the post-settle stored block is not always zero.

For any caller who locked a guess and then successfully calls settle after the target block, the reference contract always resets guesses[caller].block to 0, whereas the mutant may leave it non-zero (decremented) for some inputs, breaking that invariant.

After a successful settle by a caller who previously locked in a guess, the reference contract always resets that caller's stored block to zero, whereas the mutant may leave it non-zero (decremented), so the invariant guesses[actor].block == 0 holds for all valid inputs in reference but is violated for some inputs in the mutant.

For any actor that locked a guess and then calls settle after the target block, the correct contract always resets guesses[actor].block to 0 after settle completes; the mutant instead subtracts 1 and thus for some inputs leaves it non-zero, violating that invariant.

For any actor who successfully locked a guess and then called settle after the target block, the reference contract always leaves guesses[actor].block == 0 afterwards; the mutant that assigns guesses[actor].block = guesses[actor].block - 1 can leave it nonzero for some inputs, violating this invariant.

After a winning settle call that pays out, the reference contract resets the caller's stored guess.block to zero (so the caller cannot immediately re-settle), whereas the mutant leaves it nonzero (1) allowing the stored block to remain nonzero; the test asserts that after a successful settle the guesses[msg.sender].block == 0 (reference always) which the mutant can violate for some input.

After calling settle() the reference contract always clears the caller's stored guess.block to 0, whereas the mutant may leave it nonzero (1) for some inputs, so the property is: for every caller/sequence leading to a settle call, guesses(caller).block == 0 holds in the reference but can be false in the mutant.

For every caller that successfully calls settle (call returns without revert), the reference contract leaves the caller's stored guess.block equal to 0 (cleared), whereas the mutant sometimes leaves it as 1 causing the post-settle stored block to be nonzero.

For every caller who ever called lockInGuess and then later calls settle (whether they win or lose), the reference contract always sets their stored guesses[msg.sender].block to either 0 or a block number strictly greater than the current block (i.e. it never sets it to the concrete constant 1 after settle), but the mutant can leave it equal to the concrete constant 1 after settle for some inputs.

For every actor and sequence where they call lockInGuess then later call settle (which returns successfully), the reference contract always leaves their stored guesses[actor].block equal to 0 after settle; the mutant may leave it equal to the concrete constant 1 for some inputs so the post-settle stored block != 0 (i.e., equals 1).
